title: The effect of the MLB pitch clock
text:
The introduction of the MLB pitch clock was perhaps the most drastic and immediate rule change baseball had seen in decades. The rule change happened after the 2022 baseball season so the first season that had the pitch clock was 2023. The clock fundamentally altered the game’s famous slow cadence. Players, long accustomed to leisurely pacing and endless adjustments on the mound, were now forced into constant motion, transforming a sport once defined by patience into one defined by urgency. This single device, ticking down the seconds, did what years of debate could not. The overall goal, make the game sped up so fans pay more attention. But, someone has to have success off the rule change. Has the batter or pitcher been affected by the pitch clock change more?
To determine how overall offensive efficiency has shifted, I looked at the yearly OPS,OBP, and SLG percentages for the three years before the rule change and the three years after the change. Looking at these three statistics we can see if batters truly had an advantage since the rule change.


Code
library(tidyverse)

Code
library(ggplot2)

MLB <- read_csv("data/MLB.csv")

Code
obp <- MLB |> 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |> 
  select(Year, OBP)

slg <- MLB |> 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |> 
  select(Year, SLG)

ops <- MLB |> 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |> 
  select(Year, OPS)

MLB_stats <- MLB |> 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |> 
  select(Year, OBP, SLG, OPS) |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(OBP, SLG, OPS),
               names_to = "Statistic",
               values_to = "Value")

ggplot(MLB_stats, aes(x = factor(Year), y = Value, fill = Statistic)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("navyblue", "lightgrey", "red")) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 0.8, 0.1),  
    limits = c(0, 0.8)
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Offensive Production Holds Steady Despite the Pitch Clock",
    subtitle= "The pitch clock may have changed timing, but not results at the plate",
    caption = "By:Alex Zetterman | Source: Baseball Reference",
    x = "Season",
    y = "percentages",
    fill = "Statistic"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size=10, hjust = 0),
    legend.position = "top"
  )









At first glance, the pitch clock doesn’t seem to have shaken up offensive production. League-wide OPS, OBP, and SLG have held steady from 2020 through 2025, suggesting that hitters aren’t necessarily getting on base more or hitting for more power. But, offensive stats like OPS,OBP, and SLG only tell part of the story. The pitch clock didn’t necessarily change how much offense was involved, it just changed how teams got their offense going.
To really understand whether hitters were rushing their swings or putting more balls in play, we can look at the Contact Efficiency Ratio the number of balls in play (BIP) for every strikeout (SO). This metric shows whether faster tempo led to more action or just more whiffs.


Code
contact_eff <- MLB |>
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(
    Total_BIP = sum(BIP, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_SO = sum(SO, na.rm = TRUE),
    Contact_Efficiency = Total_BIP / Total_SO
  )

# Line chart
ggplot(contact_eff, aes(x = Year, y = Contact_Efficiency)) +
  geom_line(color = "lightblue", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 2.5) +
  
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2023, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", size = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 2023.1, y = max(contact_eff$Contact_Efficiency, na.rm = TRUE),
           label = "Pitch Clock Introduced (2023)",
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1, color = "red", size = 3, fontface = "italic") +
  
  labs(
    title = "After a 2023 Dip, Contact Rates Begin to Recover",
    subtitle = "Year-to-year changes in BIP/SO indicate gradual adaptation to pitch clock conditions",
    caption = "By:Alex Zetterman | Source: Baseball Reference",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Balls in play per strikeout",

  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size= 15),
    plot.caption = element_text(size=10, hjust = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )


Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.









When the pitch clock was first introduced in 2023, contact efficiency took an immediate dip suggesting that hitters initially struggled to adjust to the faster tempo. The sudden pace may have led to more rushed swings and fewer quality at-bats early on. However, from 2023 to 2025, the league’s Contact Efficiency Ratio climbed from around 2.82 to 2.92, showing that hitters quickly adapted to the new rhythm. This rebound suggests that while pitchers benefited early from the rule change, batters have since found their timing again, leading to more balls in play and a return to offensive balance.
After looking at how hitters adjusted, it’s equally important to examine how pitchers responded to the new pace. One of the clearest ways to see this is by comparing how often pitchers threw strikes versus balls. By charting strikeouts against walks across seasons, we can see whether the pitch clock improved pitcher command or forced them into sloppier, rushed deliveries.


Code
scatter_data <- MLB |>
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2025) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(
    BB = sum(BB, na.rm = TRUE),
    SO = sum(SO, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
ggplot(scatter_data, aes(x = BB, y = SO)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkred", size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Year), vjust = +1.3, size = 4) +
  
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(3, 3.4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(8.3, 8.8)) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Walk and Strikeout Rates Drop in Pitch-Clock Era",
    subtitle = "Faster tempo changes how pitchers and hitters approach each plate appearance",
    caption =  "By:Alex Zetterman | Source: Baseball Reference",
    x = "Walks",
    y = "Strikeouts"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 1) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 12),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.caption = element_text(size=10, hjust = 0)
  )









The scatter plot shows a clear shift after the pitch clock was introduced: both walks and strikeouts declined in the seasons that followed. Besides in 2023 when walks and strikeouts increased after the pitch-clock was introduced, so it took a year for the pitchers to get used to the change. But, for 2024 and 2025 T pitchers were working faster and relying less on deep, extended counts. The pitch clock allowed fewer walks, fewer strikeouts, and more balls put in play. This trend suggests that the pitch clock didn’t just change the pace of the game; it reshaped how pitchers approached hitters.
Overall, the data suggest that batters initially struggled when the pitch clock was introduced in 2023. Contact Efficiency dipped as hitters rushed their swings, leading to fewer quality at-bats. However, by 2025, hitters had adjusted, and BIP per strikeout rebounded, showing that batters regained their timing and were able to generate offense at similar levels as before. League-wide OPS, OBP, and SLG remained largely steady from 2020 to 2025, indicating that overall offensive production did not dramatically change, even with the faster pace.
On the pitcher side, the scatter plot shows that both walks and strikeouts decreased after the rule change, suggesting pitchers worked faster and relied less on long at-bats. While they may have gained an early advantage in 2023, by 2024–2025 their command stabilized, and the pace of the game created more balls in play rather than extreme outcomes. Taken together, this evidence indicates that hitters ultimately adapted faster, while pitchers saw only temporary gains. Therefore, while both sides felt the impact of the pitch clock, batters appear to have benefited more in the long run by adjusting successfully to the new tempo.
As every coach says, you can’t score unless you put the ball in play, and that’s exactly what batters are doing more consistently since the pitch clock change.
